question:
A 7-month-old girl is brought to the hospital by her mother, who complains of a lesion on the infant’s labia for the past 5 days. The lesion is 2 x 2 cm in size and red in color with serosanguinous fluid oozing out of the right labia. The parents note that the girl has had a history of recurrent bacterial skin infections with no pus but delayed healing since birth. She also had delayed sloughing of the umbilical cord at birth. Complete blood count results are as follows:
Neutrophils on admission  
Leukocytes 19,000/mm3
Neutrophils 83%
Lymphocytes 10%
Eosinophils 1%
Basophils 1%
Monocytes 5%
Hemoglobin 14 g/dL
Which of the following compounds is most likely to be deficient in this patient?
analysis: The clinical presentation of the 7-month-old girl, including recurrent bacterial skin infections, delayed healing, and delayed sloughing of the umbilical cord, suggests a defect in leukocyte adhesion. The elevated neutrophil count with a high percentage indicates that neutrophils are present but not effectively migrating to sites of infection. This is consistent with a deficiency in integrins, which are crucial for leukocyte adhesion and migration. Therefore, the most likely compound to be deficient in this patient is an integrin subunit.
